Providing data-driven suggestions for HR¶

Decription¶

This project is an opportunity to analyse a dataset and construct a model that'll provide insight for the HR department of a big consulting firm.

Together with this project, there'll be an executive summary detailing the key insights acquired during this analysis, that would be presented to stakeholders from Sailfort Motors. This document is the jupyter notebook that contains the complete code used for the analysis.

Objectives:¶

    1. Awnser the question made by HR: What's likely to make the employee leave the company?
    1. Clean the data according to the necessities of the analysis
    1. Create visualizations to aid in the interpretation of the relationships between the data.
    1. Construct a model and evaluate its performance.
    1. Respect the ethics considerations and data privacy.

PACE stages¶

Pace: Plan¶

Consider the questions in your PACE Strategy Document to reflect on the Plan stage.

In this stage, consider the following:

Understand the business scenario and problem¶

The HR department at Salifort Motors wants to take some initiatives to improve employee satisfaction levels at the company. They collected data from employees, but now they don’t know what to do with it. They refer to you as a data analytics professional and ask you to provide data-driven suggestions based on your understanding of the data. They have the following question: what’s likely to make the employee leave the company?

Your goals in this project are to analyze the data collected by the HR department and to build a model that predicts whether or not an employee will leave the company.

If you can predict employees likely to quit, it might be possible to identify factors that contribute to their leaving. Because it is time-consuming and expensive to find, interview, and hire new employees, increasing employee retention will be beneficial to the company.

Familiarize yourself with the HR dataset¶

The dataset that you'll be using in this lab contains 15,000 rows and 10 columns for the variables listed below.

Note: you don't need to download any data to complete this lab. For more information about the data, refer to its source on Kaggle.

Variable Description
satisfaction_level Employee-reported job satisfaction level [0–1]
last_evaluation Score of employee's last performance review [0–1]
number_project Number of projects employee contributes to
average_monthly_hours Average number of hours employee worked per month
time_spend_company How long the employee has been with the company (years)
Work_accident Whether or not the employee experienced an accident while at work
left Whether or not the employee left the company
promotion_last_5years Whether or not the employee was promoted in the last 5 years
Department The employee's department
salary The employee's salary (U.S. dollars)

The vast majority of employees are around the average of 3.3 years. There are however, some big outliers, with 6, 7, 8 and even 10 years of tenure.

In [13]:
# Determine the number of rows containing outliers

# Calculates the 25th percentile of the 'tenure' column
percentile_25 = df1['tenure'].quantile(0.25)

# Calculates the 75th percentile of the 'tenure' column
percentile_75 = df1['tenure'].quantile(0.75)

# Calculate IQR
iqr = percentile_75 - percentile_25

upper_limit = percentile_75 + 1.5 * iqr
lower_limit = percentile_25 - 1.5 * iqr
print('Lower limit:', lower_limit, 'years')
print('Upper limit:', upper_limit, 'years')

# Identify subset of data containing outliers in `tenure` and display the count of the amount of outliers
outliers = df1[(df1['tenure'] > upper_limit) | (df1['tenure'] < lower_limit)]
print('Number of outliers:', len(outliers))

Lower limit: 1.5 years
Upper limit: 5.5 years
Number of outliers: 824

Certain types of models are more sensitive to outliers than others. When you get to the stage of building your model, consider whether to remove outliers, based on the type of model you decide to use.

    1. Some columns were renamed in other to standardize them. Outliers were detected and can be easily removed if deemed necessary later and duplicates were removed, as they were most likely caused by human error.

We also perform aditional data cleaning and feature engineering during EDA, as we slowly figure out new aspects of the dataset and close in our decision for modeling construction. This process can be essential depending on the chosen model. We also need to account for bias and fairness, as the data needs to be representative and some models can tend towards bias.

Data visualizations¶

Now, examine variables that you're interested in, and create plots to visualize relationships between variables in the data.

In [15]:
# Create a plot of Average Monthly Hours vs Satisfaction Level
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.scatterplot(data=df1, x='average_monthly_hours', y='satisfaction_level', hue = 'left')
plt.title('Average Monthly Hours vs Satisfaction Level')
plt.xlabel('Average Monthly Hours')
plt.ylabel('Satisfaction Level')
line_v = plt.axvline(x=166.67, color='red')
line_h = plt.axhline(y=0.61, color='red')

# Edit the legend
handles, labels = plt.gca().get_legend_handles_labels()
new_labels = ['Stayed', 'Left', 'Avg = 166 hours/month', 'Avg = 0.61']
handles.extend([line_v, line_h])
plt.legend(handles=handles, labels=new_labels, title='Status');

This scatterplot showcases a clear, very low satisfaction score between multiple employees that worked a lot of monthly hours (240+ hours). This could be a big reason behind their decision to leave. On the other hand, we have another group of employees which left that worked below average hours (around 120-160 hours), and also have a low satisfaction score. Most of the other employees that left seem scatter randomly around the plot. The majority of the employees that stay have a good satisfaction score.

This plot has some similarities between the Average Monthly Hours vs Satisfaction Level plot. We can see that there is a group of employees on the bottom left corner that also left, and have below average monthly hours, that have a below average evaluation score. The employees that worked the longest average hours however, whereas in the previous plot most of them had extremely low satisfaction score, in this plot they have a very high evaluation score on average. It does seem however, that there is no correlation between average monthly hours and evaluation score for the employees that didn't leave.

We can see a clear difference between the average satisfaction score of employees who left vs employees who stayed. Most of the employees who left have a satisfaction score lower than average, and they reach very low scores, while most of the employees that stayed have higher than average satisfaction scores, with a low variance.

The boxplot and the histogram can showcase a relationship between the amount of average monthly hours and the number of monthly projects employees work. The higher their average amount of average monthly hours, the higher their amount of monthly projects, and the lowewr their average amount of average monthly hours, the lower their amount of monthly projects. We can also see that the vast majority of employees who worked 7 projects in a month left, and most of the employees that worked 2 projects in a month also left. This may indicate that the main cause of these 2 groups of employees leaving is that they are either overworked, or working less than what they desire.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(18, 8))

# Define custom legend handles
mean_line = plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='red', label='mean line')

# Plot 1: Employees Who Left by Evaluation Score
sns.boxplot(data=df1, x='left', y='last_evaluation', hue='left', ax=ax[0])
ax[0].set_title('Employees Who Left by Evaluation Score')
ax[0].set_xlabel('Employee status')
ax[0].set_ylabel('Evaluation Score')
ax[0].axhline(y=df1['last_evaluation'].mean(), color='red')

# Plot 2: Employees Who Left by Average Monthly Hours
sns.boxplot(data=df1, x='left', y='average_monthly_hours', hue='left', ax=ax[1])
ax[1].set_title('Employees Who Left by Average Monthly Hours')
ax[1].set_xlabel('Employee status')
ax[1].set_ylabel('Average Monthly Hours')
ax[1].axhline(y=df1['average_monthly_hours'].mean(), color='red')

# Adjust legend in both plots
for axis in ax:
    handles, _ = axis.get_legend_handles_labels()
    handles[0].set_label('stayed')
    handles[1].set_label('left')
    handles.append(mean_line)
    axis.legend(handles=handles)

In the first plot, there is higher variance between the evaluation score of employees who left compared to those who stayed. Other than that, they seem pretty similar. It might be the case that employees who left and worked 240+ hours monthly on average were the one with higher than average evaluation score, while the ones that left and worked 110-150 hours monthly on average were the ones with lower than average evaluation scores. The second plot plot is very similar to the previous one, showing more evidence that the evaluation scores from employees who left might have a strong correlation with their average monthly hours.

Seeing as the vast majority of employees who left were not promoted, despite the fact that their average tenure is longer that those who stayed, this may be another key reason why they left. Most of these employees may have been expecting promotions after 3,5 years of work, and after not getting one, they sought out different positions in other companies.

Insights¶

  • The satisfaction_level column had the highest negative correlation with the left column. This means that employees with lower satisfaction levels are likely to leave. Most of the employees who left had below average satisfaction levels.
  • The vast majority of employees who left were not promoted, meaning this may be another big factor behind their decision.
  • Most of the employees who left fall in 2 categories: Overworked and underworked. They are eihter working much more hours averagely per month than average (240-300 hours), or considerably less (120-150 hours). This also reflects on the amount of projects they work per month. Most employees that had 2 projects in a month left, and almost all of the emplyees that had 7 projects in a month left.
  • There is no significant difference between departments.
  • When analyzing only the employees who left, some variables have very high multicolinearity, demonstrating that some of the employees that leave can be easily identified following their work behavior and history.

paCe: Construct Stage¶

  • Determine which models are most appropriate
  • Construct the model
  • Confirm model assumptions
  • Evaluate model results to determine how well your model fits the data

🔎

Recall model assumptions¶

Logistic Regression model assumptions

  • Outcome variable is categorical: The outcome variable is the left column, which is binary. This assumption is met
  • Observations are independent of each other: No observation influences or predict any other observation. This assumption is met
  • No severe multicollinearity among X variables: There is multicollinearity between some of the x variables. However, they are weak, meaning it should not affect the outcome too much. This assumption is met
  • No extreme outliers: The extreme outliers will be removed before the model construction. This assumption is met
  • Linear relationship between each X variable and the logit of the outcome variable. We can verify this assumption by seeing how each X variable affects the outcome variable. This assumption is met
  • Sufficiently large sample size. The dataset contains 10 columns and almost 12.000 rows. This assumption is met

💭

Step 3. Model Building, Step 4. Results and Evaluation¶

  • Fit a model that predicts the outcome variable using two or more independent variables
  • Check model assumptions
  • Evaluate the model

Identify the type of prediction task.¶

The goal for this analysis is to construct a model that aims to predict when employees will leave the company. This is a binary variable, where 0 indicates the employee is in the company, and 1 indicates the employee left.

Identify the types of models most appropriate for this task.¶

Considering the binary nature of the "left" variable, a logistic regression is a good model for predicting whether or not employees will leave. If the logistic regression results are deemed inaccurate or insufficient, then a decision tree or a random forest model will be used instead.

1st model: Logisitc Regression¶

A Logisitc Regression will be performed with the 'left' column as our observed variable, and every other column as features. A binomial logistic regression suits the task because it involves binary classification.

Before splitting the data into training and test data, we'll need to encode the 'salary' and 'departmente' variables, as those are non-numeric.

This is a very strong AUC score, meaning the model can predict employees who will leave very well. Next, we'll write a function that will help you extract all the scores from the grid search.

In [40]:
def make_results(model_name:str, model_object, metric:str):
    '''
    Arguments:
        model_name (string): what you want the model to be called in the output table
        model_object: a fit GridSearchCV object
        metric (string): precision, recall, f1, accuracy, or auc
  
    Returns a pandas df with the F1, recall, precision, accuracy, and auc scores
    for the model with the best mean 'metric' score across all validation folds.  
    '''

    # Create dictionary that maps input metric to actual metric name in GridSearchCV
    metric_dict = {'auc': 'mean_test_roc_auc',
                   'precision': 'mean_test_precision',
                   'recall': 'mean_test_recall',
                   'f1': 'mean_test_f1',
                   'accuracy': 'mean_test_accuracy'
                  }

    # Get all the results from the CV and put them in a df
    cv_results = pd.DataFrame(model_object.cv_results_)

    # Isolate the row of the df with the max(metric) score
    best_estimator_results = cv_results.iloc[cv_results[metric_dict[metric]].idxmax(), :]

    # Extract Accuracy, precision, recall, and f1 score from that row
    auc = best_estimator_results.mean_test_roc_auc
    f1 = best_estimator_results.mean_test_f1
    recall = best_estimator_results.mean_test_recall
    precision = best_estimator_results.mean_test_precision
    accuracy = best_estimator_results.mean_test_accuracy
  
    # Create table of results
    table = pd.DataFrame()
    table = pd.DataFrame({'model': [model_name],
                          'precision': [precision],
                          'recall': [recall],
                          'F1': [f1],
                          'accuracy': [accuracy],
                          'auc': [auc]
                        })
  
    return table

All of these scores from the decision tree model are strong indicators of good model performance and better than the previous Logistic Regression. Recall that decision trees can be vulnerable to overfitting, and random forests avoid overfitting by incorporating multiple trees to make predictions. However, seeing as random forests require more computational power, take longer to complete and has a longer code, the decision tree will be the definitive model.

Decision Tree - round 2¶

There is a chance that there is some data leakage occurring. Data leakage is when you use data to train your model that should not be used during training, either because it appears in the test data or because it's not data that you'd expect to have when the model is actually deployed. Training a model with leaked data can give an unrealistic score that is not replicated in production. In this case, it's likely that the company won't have satisfaction levels reported for all of its employees. It's also possible that the average_monthly_hours column is a source of some data leakage. If employees have already decided upon quitting, or have already been identified by management as people to be fired, they may be working fewer hours.

The first round of decision tree and random forest models included all variables as features. This round will incorporate feature engineering to build improved models. We'll proceed by dropping satisfaction_level and creating a new feature that roughly captures whether an employee is overworked. It will be a binary variable.

pacE: Execute Stage¶

  • Interpret model performance and results
  • Share actionable steps with stakeholders

✏

Recall evaluation metrics¶

  • AUC is the area under the ROC curve; it's also considered the probability that the model ranks a random positive example more highly than a random negative example.
  • Precision measures the proportion of data points predicted as True that are actually True, in other words, the proportion of positive predictions that are true positives.
  • Recall measures the proportion of data points that are predicted as True, out of all the data points that are actually True. In other words, it measures the proportion of positives that are correctly classified.
  • Accuracy measures the proportion of data points that are correctly classified.
  • F1-score is an aggregation of precision and recall.

💭

Some of the data collected could be more tailored towards model construction, such as the salary variable having the actual salary of the employees or a numerical range. Other factors that may affect the decision of employees leaving, such as employees' relationship with coworkers and management could also be measured and addded to the data. A feedback loop can also be establish in order to incorporate new data and evolving business needs into the model. This would ensure continuous relevance and accuracy.

Step 4. Results and Evaluation¶

  • Interpret model
  • Evaluate model performance using metrics
  • Prepare results, visualizations, and actionable steps to share with stakeholders

Summary of model results¶

  • Logistic Regression

The logistic regression model achieved a precision of 79%, recall of 82%, f1-score of 80% (all weighted averages), and accuracy of 83%.

  • Tree-based Machine Learning

After conducting feature engineering, the decision tree model achieved AUC of 95%, precision of 85%, recall of 90%, f1-score of 87%, and accuracy of 95%, on the test set.

Conclusion, Recommendations, Next Steps¶

Most of the employees are leaving due to their average monthly work hours either being too high or too low. A system should be implemented to make sure employees are working a minimum and a maximum amount of monthly hours close to the average of 166 hours.

The number of hours per month has a very high correlation with the amount of projects they work on, so they should also be tailored.

With an AUC score of 0.95 after conducting feature engineering, the Decision Tree model performs very well, and can be used appropriately with more data. Caution should still be exercised when introducing new data due to bias.
